facts.claim: The title: if you ask your mom whether your business idea is good she will usually say yes, because she wants to support you. The book's point is that almost anyone can give you misleading answers, often without meaning to (not wanting to hurt you, not knowing their own preferences, nothing at stake).
Three rules: talk about their life instead of your idea; ask about specific past events instead of generics or opinions about the future; talk less and listen more.
'They own the problem, you own the solution.'
Bad question: 'Do you think my idea for a product that does X is any good?' Better: ask how they handle X today, what products they use, what problems they hit.
Bad question: 'Would you buy a product that did X?' Better: find out whether X is a real pain or something they mostly ignore, and how they solve it now.
Bad question: 'How much would you pay for a product that did X?' Better: ask how much time and money X costs them now and whether they have paid for past solutions; or ask for a pre-order.
'Once you start talking about your idea, they stop talking about their problems.'
'If they haven't looked for ways of solving it already, they're not going to look for (or buy) yours.'
Good questions listed: 'Talk me through the last time X happened'; 'Why do you bother with X?'; 'What else have you tried for X?'; 'Who else should I talk to?'
Chapter 2 names three kinds of bad data: compliments, fluff, and ideas.

'Compliments are the fool's gold of customer learning: shiny, distracting, and worthless.' The fix: do not accept the compliment, dig for facts: why they like it, what else they have tried, what it cost them.

Fluff has three forms: generic claims ('I usually', 'I always', 'I never'), future-tense promises ('I will', 'I would'), and hypotheticals ('I might', 'I could'). The most dangerous is 'I would definitely buy that'; steer back to the last time they ran into the problem.
Ideas and feature requests: when someone asks for a feature, find the underlying problem, their current workaround and motivation; 'Why do you want that?'.
Commitment and advancement: a meeting counts only if the customer gives up something they value (time, reputation or money) and moves to the next real step of the sales funnel.

Commitment types: time (a scheduled next meeting, feedback on wireframes, a trial), reputation (an introduction to a decision maker or teammate, a public testimonial), money (letter of intent, pre-order, deposit).
'If you don't know what happens next after a product or sales meeting, the meeting was pointless.' and 'The more they're giving up, the more seriously you can take what they're saying.'
Bad meeting endings: 'Looks great, let me know when it launches!' and 'I would definitely buy that.' Good ones: 'When can we start the trial?' and 'Can I buy the prototype?'
Money is not required early on: in first meetings a commitment of time or an introduction can do; one quoted good ending is 'There are a couple people I can introduce you to...'.
Good question list also includes: 'Why do you bother with X?', 'What else have you tried for X?', 'Who else should I talk to?'
